name: Ziheche (dried human placenta)

lead: Ziheche is the traditional Chinese medicine name for dried human placenta. In that tradition it is a tonic said to nourish qi and blood and the liver and kidney, and it is linked to anti-aging aims.

The appearance payoff is claimed vitality and youthfulness. Research has examined placenta-derived products from animals, such as cow and camel placenta peptides, in laboratory aging models, while studies of the human product are limited and placentophagy reviews report no documented benefit.

paras: Traditionally the dried placenta is prepared as a powder, pill or ingredient in herbal formulas. Modern placenta capsules are a related practice.

The CDC reported an infant infection with group B Streptococcus linked to a mother's placenta capsules and advised against ingesting them. A 2018 review advised clinicians to discourage placentophagy as potentially harmful.

angle.text: Traditional practitioners describe ziheche as a blood and qi tonic. Aging-related and skin claims come from that tradition and from related placenta extract research.

lead: Ziheche is dried human placenta used in traditional Chinese medicine. It has been used in some formulas for wasting disease, infertility and impotence, according to Wikipedia [1]. In research papers it is described as a tonic that supplements qi and blood and nourishes liver and kidney, and placenta extracts have been explored for delaying aging [2].

In looks terms, the tradition links it to vitality and a youthful condition. Laboratory work reports anti-aging and anti-wrinkle peptide activity in placenta from other species, such as camel placenta, whose anti-skin-aging activity was screened in a 2026 study [3].

paras: Ziheche appears in traditional formulas and in modern Chinese patent medicines. A network meta-analysis of Chinese patent medicines combined with hormone therapy for premature ovarian failure is among the clinical literature on such products [4].

No studies found on dried human placenta for appearance. Related laboratory work includes cow placenta extract in a liver-aging model [2], camel placenta peptides screened for anti-skin-aging activity in vitro [3], and an older mouse study of ziheche on anemia and blood-cell recovery [5]. A 2018 review of placentophagy advised clinicians to discourage it as potentially harmful with no documented benefit [1].
The CDC reported a newborn with group B Streptococcus infection likely linked to the mother's placenta capsules and advised avoiding capsule ingestion [1].
